Memory Applicability Guard.

A decision-support prototype for checking whether stored memory should shape an agent's next answer or action.

RoleIndependent projectPeriodMay—August 2026StackPython · JSON · Unit tests
MEMORY GUARD / DECISION MAPCONTEXT → ACTION
UUseCURRENT + RELEVANT
IIgnoreSTALE OR REVOKED
AAskEVIDENCE GAP

The case / 03

Long-term memory can make an assistant more useful, but a remembered preference or permission may be outdated, unrelated, or revoked. The prototype makes that decision explicit before the memory influences a recommendation or action.

Illustrative case

An old note says a user allowed an action; the current request revokes that permission. The guard should ignore the old permission and explain why it cannot guide the next step.

What I built

I created a research-informed Python decision helper that evaluates a candidate memory against the present request and returns a structured result. Its response distinguishes when to use the memory, ignore it, or ask the user for clarification.

The helper separates the memory action — USE, IGNORE, or ASK — from the recommendation for the underlying task. It also records the decisive evidence, reason code, and next step so the decision can be inspected rather than inferred from a final answer.

Two decisions, kept separate

  • Should this memory influence the task? Current scope, permission, recency, and evidence determine its applicability.
  • What should the agent do next? The helper can recommend proceeding, revising, asking the user, verifying an external fact, or escalating for review.

Decisions that mattered

  • Check applicability before personalization. A fact can be true and still be irrelevant to the current task.
  • Respect changed permissions. Revoked instructions must not quietly survive as an old preference.
  • Make uncertainty visible. When evidence is missing, the safer decision is often to clarify.

Validation and limits

The helper is packaged as an installable agent skill and checked with deterministic tests. In the frozen v0.7 experiment, the tested memory approach did not outperform its baseline: both scored 110/128. That result shaped this project as an auditable review workflow rather than an autonomous safety claim.

It is a research-informed decision-support prototype, not a production-validated system. The diagram above describes the memory decision branches rather than showing a live interface.
